title: The Manifest
subtitle: Data Wrangling Assignment · group_by + summarise
story: Your wine ship arrives in Alexandria at first light, Pharos Lighthouse still burning gold above the harbor. You came in with a cargo — a hold of amphorae from the Aegean islands — and by the law of the port no ship may leave until two things are done: the cargo must be registered with the city, every amphora grouped by origin and accurately tallied; and the great Pharos light turned upon the ship to clear it for the open sea. The tide turns at dusk. Reconcile the manifest room by room, climb to the lantern, swing the light onto your ship, the set loose your sail to escape before the water leaves without you.

done.title: The manifest is reconciled!
done.body: When considering the quality on a varietal-by-varietal basis it is Thasos, not Chios, that gives the truest wine — the correction goes down in the register and the tally is stamped true. Now, go down to the harbour and turn the great lamp to shine on your ship so you can leave port!

plannedHotspots.label: The count-board
plannedHotspots.body:
Every amphora that comes off the ship is notched here, one cut for one jar. It is the plainest operation in the port and the first sigil a clerk learns: ⦀ the tally — how many are in a pile? Set a tray of goods into piles and the tally is read off the fullest pile: nothing about what the pieces are worth, only how many of them stand together.

The manifest itself is the ship's register of the cargo: one line per amphora, each carrying its island and its grape alongside the measurements taken at the press. More is written down than any single question needs, so the trick is choosing the right column.

plannedHotspots.label: The price-board
plannedHotspots.body:
The day's lots are chalked up in order of what they will fetch, the dearest riding highest on the board. That is the second sigil: ▲ the greatest — what does the richest pile come to? A pile's worth is the numbers on its pieces added together, and the greatest is the total carried by the heaviest pile — the figure itself, never the pile's name.

Wine is priced by the grape here rather than by the island, because the grape is what decides how strong the pressing runs, and strength is what the buyers are paying for. The register carries the grape of every amphora alongside its measured strength.

pick.prompt: The market prices wine by the grape, and the strongest pressings fetch the most — so the cargo's whole value hangs on one question. Which grape in the hold yields the most potent wine? Click it on the board.

p <- ggplot(dplyr::summarise(dplyr::group_by(wine_cargo, varietal),
                             mean_alcohol = mean(alcohol)),
            aes(reorder(varietal, mean_alcohol), mean_alcohol)) +
     ggiraph::geom_col_interactive(aes(data_id = varietal, tooltip = varietal)) +
     coord_flip() +
     labs(x = NULL, y = "Mean alcohol (%)")
pick.hint: One grape stands clear of the rest — that is the one the price-board would chalk highest.

question.prompt:
The ledgers set the trouble down plainly: the islands do not ship the same grapes. Chios sends mostly its noble varieties and Thasos mostly its common ones, so a plain average flatters the famous name and tells you about the packing, not the ground.

The tally on the desk is the merchant's version, and it is the one you wrote in the market. Repair it so that every grape has an equal say in each island's figure — then say which island truly makes the better wine.

feedback.correct: Correct — noted in your field notebook: give every grape an equal say and Thasos leads at 7.43, with Chios falling to last at 6.26.
wrong: Work it in two stages. Take one average for each island-and-grape pairing first, so a common grape and a noble one each contribute a single figure.
Then release the grouping and average those per-pairing figures within each island — every grape now counts once, however many jars of it were packed.
Two summarise steps: mean quality per island-and-grape, then the mean of those per island. The leader is not the island that led in the market.

Three marks were struck into the bronze board with a number beside each (▲ 17, ⦀ 5, ▼ 10) and the nine seals in your hands could be sorted by colour, by shape or by size. Each mark named a summary, and for each one only a single grouping produces that figure. Group by size and the largest pile totals 17 (3 + 6 + 8): that is ▲. Three groupings, three summaries, one door: group_by + summarise with the code stripped away and the answer set in bronze.

debrief.title: How this world worked
debrief.intro: The whole day in Alexandria was one skill wearing a harbour for a costume: group_by + summarise. The scenario asks you to sort many things into piles by a shared trait, then read one number off each pile. Every room binned your cargo a different way and read one summary from it; the Library showed you what happens when the piles are not built fairly; and the bronze door at the top of the lighthouse opened only when you grouped a collection you had gathered yourself, three different ways, and read the right figure off each. Here is how each part embodied the wrangling.
